newsitem.title: USA: American Axle pact appears headed for approval.
newsitem.headline: American Axle pact appears headed for approval.

text.p: A new labor contract that gives union workers at American Axle & Manufacturing Inc. the same basic terms as Big Three autoworkers appeared headed for ratification Monday, with approval ratings running in the high-90-percent range.
United Auto Workers officials would not release the totals because all the votes had not been counted.
But voting had been mostly completed at four UAW locals in Tonawanda and Buffalo, N.Y.; Three Rivers, Mich., and Detroit, by late Monday afternoon, according to a source close to the situation.
Voting at Local 235 at the company's main plant in Detroit was still continuing. Approval by 50 percent of the approximately 7,200 UAW members at American Axle is needed for the tentative contract.

American Axle, which was spun off from General Motors Corp. in 1994, supplies virtually all of the axles for GM pickup trucks and sport utilitiy vehicles, as well as axle shafts for Ford Motor Co. and a small number of parts to Chrysler Corp.

Susan Davis, vice president of Local 262 in Detroit, said terms of the three-year agreement "technically" follow the pattern set by the Big Three automakers during contract bargaining last fall. She declined to provide more details because voting was still taking place.

That means American Axle workers will receive a $2,000 lump sum payment in the first year, followed by annual increases of 3 percent in the second and third years. The Big Three pact also guarantees jobs for 95 percent of the current work force.

American Axle, however, is believed to have received some concessions in the form of a longer grow-in rate for new workers and lower starting wages, sources said. Under the Big Three contract, new workers are hired at 70 percent of the starting base hourly wage of about $19, and take three years to reach parity.
A company spokesman declined to comment.
After a weekend of marathon bargaining, a new contract was reached early Feb. 17, minutes before a union-imposed strike deadline.

The talks were closely followed by the industry because they mark the first time a GM spin-off has had to negotiate a new labor agreement. American Axle had agreed to honor terms of the 1993-96 agreement when the spin-off occurred.
